It is not a generic copula or perception detector: 'the color of the car was' (0.00), 'the method/design/result of the study was' (0.9-1.5) and the literal 'I see the cat' (0.00) stay near zero, and the peak is identical (3.47) whether the copula is followed by a purpose clause ('to compare') or by 'unclear'.

Sediment cores pulled from the estuary in the spring of 2019 showed that the marsh had been shrinking for at least four decades, and that the loss accelerated sharply after the flood barrier was built upstream. Researchers at the coastal station spent the next two years mapping the channels that feed the marsh, setting sediment traps along the main creek, and comparing their measurements with aerial photographs held in the county archive. The photographs, some of them taken from a light aircraft in the 1970s, turned out to be far more detailed than anyone expected. They recorded the position of every creek mouth, the width of every mudflat, and the seasonal extent of the eelgrass beds. When the field team overlaid the modern survey on the historical images, a pattern that no one had described before became visible. The marsh was not simply eroding along its outer edge, as the earlier reports had assumed. It was also losing elevation from within, because the sediment that once arrived with each spring tide was now trapped behind the barrier or dredged out of the navigation channel before it could settle.

The central objective of the restoration program is to reconnect the marsh to the sediment supply that the barrier cut off, so that the surface can rise fast enough to keep pace with the rising sea. Engineers proposed a series of controlled breaches in the old dike, each sized to admit a measured volume of water on the highest tides while keeping the farmland behind it dry during ordinary storms. The proposal drew objections from several landowners, who worried that salt water would reach their wells, and from a few biologists, who argued that the breaches should be opened gradually so that the eelgrass could adapt to the changed salinity. A compromise emerged after a second winter of monitoring: two small breaches in the first year, a third in the second, and a review of the well data before any further openings were approved.

The monitoring plan attached to the permit runs for a decade and requires the county to publish every dataset it collects, including the cores, the water levels and the counts of juvenile fish. That requirement matters more than it might appear, because earlier restoration efforts in the region were never evaluated and the lessons from them were lost when the responsible agency was reorganised. Members of the review panel said they would judge the project less on the first year of photographs than on whether the marsh surface actually gained elevation by the fifth. If it did not, the panel would recommend closing the breaches and returning the site to the farmers, an outcome that almost nobody involved expects. The county has already hired two field technicians to run the surveys, and the first of the quarterly reports is due in the spring.
